Lysistrata. Aristophanes' farcical antiwar comedy, performed in 411 BCE, right in the middle of the Peloponnesian War's twenty-year grind. The play features perhaps the most audacious political weapon ever conceived: an organized sex strike.

Lysistrata, an Athenian woman, has a radical idea. The war between Athens and Sparta has been devastating both cities for two decades. So she organizes the women across hostile Greek city-states to refuse sexual relations with their husbands until peace is negotiated. The men, sexually frustrated and desperate, quickly sue for peace.

But the women do more than withhold sex. They seize the Acropolis and control its treasury, preventing their husbands from funding further military campaigns. It's a brilliant two-pronged political strategy: cut off the pleasure and the purse strings.

The play is gleefully bawdy. The male actors wear comedic phallus costumes, exaggerated symbols of frustrated military masculinity. The chorus splits between old men defending the war and old women supporting peace, staging what amounts to an ideological mock battle. Through all of it, Aristophanes poses a serious question: what does endless war actually serve? Does it benefit the state, or has it become an obsession divorced from reason?

The resolution is pure fantasy—female coordinated action ends male militarism—yet it was radical propaganda for something both democratic and subversive: women's collective power. The play mocks Athenian and Spartan leaders alike, hinting at the war's desperation in its final years. Lysistrata works not because the fantasy is realistic, but because the question underlying it was impossible to ignore. The audience was watching a world on fire, and Aristophanes was asking them: what if the solution was right in front of you, if you would only listen to the people you've been ignoring?
